sections.text: यातयामं गतरसं पूति पर्युषितं च यत्।
The Ignorant love food which is stale, not nourishing, putrid and corrupt, the leavings of others and unclean.
Sacrifice is Pure when it is offered by one who does not covet the fruit thereof, when it is done according to the commands of scripture, and with implicit faith that the sacrifice is a duty.
अभिसन्धाय तु फलं दम्भार्थमपि चैव यत्।
Sacrifice which is performed for the sake of its results, or for self-glorification - that, O best of Aryans, is the product of Passion.

We had been discussing chapter 17, Shraddha Traya Vibhaga Yoga, three types of sraddhas. Culturally we are obsessed with classifications, so we classify everything. In this case, Arjuna asked the question: if somebody does not have any guidance from the Sastras -- either voluntarily rejected or not available -- but he still has faith and is working, propelled by his faith, what type of faith is that? Bhagavan says: as the man, so is his faith; also, as the faith, so is the man. Both have a very synergistic relationship.
My faith and who I am are basically very closely related to each other. And therefore this chapter is all about explaining the types of faith one can develop. If I have a goal to be one type of a person or other, I should examine what type of faith do I have? Or I should at least see that what type of faith will lead me to the goal which I want to achieve. So therefore the whole discussion about the three types of faith, and obviously it was quite anticipated after learning 16 chapters of Bhagavad Gita, that these three types of faith correspond with the three qualities of Maya, Sattva, Rajas and Tamas. Everything can be the Sattvik, Rajasik or Tamasic.
Once again we have to remember that nothing we have discussed ever said that one quality can be exclusive of other two. The one quality always comes with the little shades of the other two. But it is the predominance of my personality or my faith makes me who I am. The worship people do are also depending on their faith. Sattvicas will worship the Devas -- in other words, to get the illumination of their mind. They want the light of knowledge in their internal instruments. The Rajasic wants to achieve wealth, prosperity, something they think will give them infinite happiness. But we know it is transitory.
The goal is the same for all of us: liberation from our sorrows and unhappiness. We should examine whether my path is the one which will lead me to that goal. And therefore the discussion. Even the likes and dislikes of people depend on their personality, their faith. The type of food I like depends on which mood my mind is in.
So when Im in a sattvic mode, the type of food I like will be what we discussed. Sighnaha rasaha, that which promotes health. When Im in rajasik mood, something which tastes good and when Im tamasik mood, whatever is available now, this mood continues to change in our day to day life. Also, at times I would love to listen to Jagjit Singhs ghazal. But there are times I shut him off -- this is not the time.
Im sometimes driving for like a couple of hours. You normally think that Ill be putting Jagjit Singh ghazal or two hours. I never listen to it. I want to listen to Bloomberg or CNBC or something which keeps my mind alert about this world. Because Im not in a mood of listening to music. So mood of my mind determines what I like and dislike.
This mood continues to change. But my goal is to make sure the predominance of my mind is in the one or the other which I am currently convinced that which gives me the liberation from my sorrow. And therefore this elaborate discussion about these three faiths: aphalakankshi bhih yajnaha. We have seen what they worship, what types of likes and dislikes they have and therefore what they receive, the ahara, what they eat, what they receive through their senses. Type of music I like. All that is depending on the mood of my mind.
So now it says what type of yajna, the actions. Yajna basically is a sacrifice. When we sacrifice something we are offering to someone. Every action of mine in this world is my Yajna, my offering to this world. But whether Im offering with expectations or no expectations is what makes that action either a yajna or a normal action.
So Aphalakankshi bhih Yajnah Vidhidrishtah ya ijyate Yastavyam eveti manah samadhaya sa Sattvikah. That yajna or sacrifice which is offered without desire for fruits and performed as per the ordinance -- in other words, done methodically. I can do something haphazardly or I can do something methodically. Both will have different results. You know, when I first went to architecture school, the first thing they teach you -- well, they dont teach you, actually, you have to learn on your own.
In those days we used to have drawing boards. You put a paper on it and then you have T-squares and set squares -- those of you in engineering understand. For the first two months, I never understood how to do that, because nobody ever tells you how to align this paper. So you haphazardly start something and it never really comes out right. One day I had to ask my seniors. One of my friends, who was a senior student -- I said: you know, Gupta, this never comes out right. All my borders are always off.
He said: Rajan, let me tell you how to do it. First thing, you set your board correctly. Then make sure your seat is comfortable so you can reach everything. Then align your paper to your T-square, not to your board. And that was like an eye-opener to me -- oh, thats why his drawing comes out better than mine.
Because when I was putting the effort before, without Vidhi Purvakam, I had never tried to find out what is the right method, or at least had no knowledge of it. Once I found out the right method, then I realized why it is so important. Before you start, make sure everything is correct -- drawing board is stable, my seat is stable, nothing is falling apart, everything is aligned. Now things work out much better than before.
So Bhagavan said, one who is doing Vidhi Purvakam -- Vidhi Drishtah, Yastavyam Eveti Manah Samadhaya Sa Sattvikah -- with the firm faith that sacrifice is a duty. Why am I doing it? Because we always say: well, if I dont have any desire for fruits, then there is no motivation -- why would I be doing anything? If I say you go to work but there is no expectation for a paycheck at the end of the month, what is the motivation? Bhagavan said, its the other way around. The paycheck should be the byproduct of your actions, and you have to be absolutely certain it will be there, because you have faith in the law of karma.
The law of karma says your actions will be rewarded appropriately. One of the persons I interviewed long, long, long time ago when I was in Nairobi -- I would never forget him. I never hired him, but I still never forget him. I asked him: what salary do you expect? And he said: whatever you think is appropriate is good for me. And then he added: I believe that whatever Im worth, Ill get paid, whether by this employer or the next one.
You may underpay me today, but my next employer will recognize my worth and will pay me for it. I will never forget him. A complete faith in his ability, and that his worth will be paid for. Bhagavan said, if you have that faith then only motivation you have to do your work is that this is my duty. That duty boundness is your motivation. I am a human being and therefore this is my duty. Im a part of this community, therefore this is my duty.
Im part of this nation as a citizen. Therefore this is my duty. You take a role upon yourself and then see what your duty is and see whether youre performing those duties. And all your actions, because of the role youve taken, now motivate you to perform them. When you become a father, when you become a mother -- previously you were just a guy.
Now you are a husband and then you are a father. Your duties continue to evolve and see whether you are motivated by those additional duties which you have taken upon yourself by taking this role. Bhagavan says the one who is performing these Yajnas in this world, performing sacrifices, offering their actions -- first of all, no predetermined expectation for the results. The results will be there. If I put actions, results will be there.
But what that would be I do not know. Because the results are always in future. Actions are always in present. Results are always in somebodys control. Because if I act in this world, the world will react. So its in control of the world.
Actions are always in my control. With that understanding I will not dissipate my energy in worrying about the results but use all my energy into my actions. Therefore my actions will be better. And therefore my results will be better. I have figured out my duty is this and also took some guidance. Therefore, you become the first-time mom -- all those books, and then you take seminars. Thats why Im so fascinated. When my son Neeraj was born, I was completely unprepared for everything. When he was born I was working in my office because my father in law called me and said I think they had taken Meena to whatever the room. You can come as quickly as you can. I took no hurry part very seriously.
So by the time I reached there, he was already born. If you take guidance, then you will do things right. And obviously Meena never let me forget that, even today. So that is the result of my lack of Vidhi Purvakam. And then with a complete faith that this is what I want to do because this is my duty. And see such an action is satvikaha.
Such a yajna is Sattvic Yajna. All my actions -- if I define and say Aphalakankshi, in other words no predetermined result -- I have decided: I go for an interview, and all the time I remember my job is to just go and present myself. Whether they select me or not is their problem. So I come back and Jackie asks: so how was the interview? The interview is always good -- it is the result you have to worry about.
So aphalakankshi, vidhi drishta -- sattvic actions and yajnas are like that. Dont have any expectations. Do it because thats your duty and then be firm that thats what you want to do. Abhisandhaya tu phalam -- the next verse contrasts with this. In the first one we are doing it simply because it is my duty. I dont have a predetermined notion of what results will be, and Im firmly established in that action.
Abhisandhaya tu Phalam -- the next one is similar but with a slight difference. In the first one, I had no expectations. Here, I want to make sure that if I do this, I want to get this thing out of it. Before I make a donation, I ask: what kind of recognition will your organization give me? Can I get a seat on your board, or what other things are you going to do for us? Any action where I want to have a predetermined result -- that is Abhisandhaya tu Phalam. Dambhartham api cha eva yat -- Im doing it because I want to show off. Let me give a concert where Im going to show off how good a singer I am.
Ijjyatai Bharata Sreshta Vidhirajasam There are only two motivation I have in performing these actions. One is I want to show off and acquire something which is predetermined. Therefore that motivates me.

These verses complete the teaching on food and introduce the three types of yajna (sacrifice or action). Tamasic food is described as yatayamam gatarasam puti paryusitam - stale, tasteless, putrid, and leftover - reflecting a careless, inert approach to life. But the heart of this section lies in understanding sattvic versus rajasic action. The sattvic yajna is performed aphalakankibhih (without desire for fruits), following proper method (vidhi-drsta), with the firm conviction that this is my duty (yastavyam eva). The rajasic yajna, by contrast, is performed abhisandhaya tu phalam dambhartham - with expectation of results and for the sake of showing off.
Reflect on your motivations at work and in service. When you take on a project, do you first calculate whats in it for me? (rajasic) or do you recognize it as your duty and trust that appropriate results will follow (sattvic)? Krishnas teaching here connects to the law of karma: if you have faith that your worth will be recognized - if not by this employer, then by another - you can focus entirely on excellence rather than anxiety about rewards. This week, choose one task and approach it purely as duty, without mental bargaining about recognition or reward. Notice how this shifts your energy and the quality of your work. Ask yourself: Am I performing this action to show off my abilities, or because it genuinely needs to be done?
